SOURCE familyroots.in (Omkareshwar — The Fourth Jyotirlinga · FamilyRoots):
Omkareshwar takes its name from Om itself, the primal sacred syllable — and the temple's island, formed by the Narmada river splitting around it, is traditionally said to be shaped like the Om symbol when viewed from above, making the geography itself part of the sanctity.
Its central legend belongs to a king already present in this site's own genealogical database: Mandhata, a ruler of the Suryavamsha (Solar Dynasty) whose line runs back through Ikshvaku, the dynasty founder covered in The Celestial Dynasties.
King Mandhata's Penance
Mandhata, a celebrated king of the Suryavamsha line, is said to have performed intense penance on this river island seeking Shiva's favor — accounts vary on whether his purpose was to secure victory over powerful enemies, to be granted the strength to rule justly over the whole earth, or simply devotion for its own sake. Pleased with the king's austerity, Shiva manifested there as a Jyotirlinga, and the site came to be called Mandhata or Mandhata Parvat after the king whose devotion drew Shiva to remain.
Because Mandhata belongs to the same Suryavamsha line already traced in this site's Celestial Dynasties series and its wider genealogical database, this is one of the more direct genealogical bridges the Jyotirlinga legends offer back into the site's own core project — a king already documented as an ancestor, here shown at one specific devotional moment in his reign.
The Vindhya Mountain's Pride
A second, older legend is also closely associated with this site, explaining not the temple's founding directly but the origin of the lingam Vindhya himself is said to have worshipped here. The Vindhya mountain range, envious of Mount Meru's cosmic stature at the center of the world, performed severe penance to Shiva asking to grow taller than any other mountain. Shiva granted the boon.
Vindhya's growth did not stop at reasonable bounds — he continued rising until he began blocking the path of the sun and moon across the sky, throwing the cosmic order into disorder. The sage Agastya was asked to intervene: traveling south, he asked Vindhya, as a gesture of respect to a revered teacher, to bow down and remain low until Agastya returned from his journey. Vindhya complied out of reverence — and Agastya, by design, never returned north, settling permanently in the south instead. Vindhya, bound by his word, has remained lower than Meru ever since.
In the version of the story tied to this site, it was during his penance that Vindhya is said to have worshipped a lingam of sand or clay at this location on the Narmada — the same site later associated with Mandhata's own penance and the manifestation of the Jyotirlinga proper. The two legends sit side by side in local tradition rather than being fully merged into one continuous narrative.
Some traditions count Omkareshwar and a second, nearby lingam called Amareshwar (or Mamleshwar, on the opposite riverbank) as together forming the single Jyotirlinga counted in the traditional twelve — treating the pair as one site with two shrines rather than fully separate locations. This article follows the majority convention of treating Omkareshwar as the primary named site of the twelve.
Today

ओंकारेश्वर से जुड़ी दूसरी कथा के अनुसार एक बार विंध्याचल पर्वत ने खुद को सबसे ऊँचा और महान होने के लिए भगवान शिव का तप प्रारंभ किया, क्योंकि उस समय सुमेरु पर्वत सबसे ऊँचा और बड़ा माना जाता था. मान्यता है कि विंध्याचल के कठिन तप से प्रसन्न होकर महादेव ने उसे वरदान दिया कि वह अपनी मर्जी से बढ़ सके, लेकिन साथ ही उसे अपनी शक्ति का दुरुपयोग न करने की शर्त भी रखी.

मान्यता है कि उसी समय वहां मौजूद ऋषि-मुनियों के अनुरोध पर महादेव ने ओंकारेश्वर नामक लिंग को दो भाग में बांट दिया. जिसमें से एक ओंकारेश्वर और दूसरा ममलेश्वर कहलाया. दो अलग-अलग लिंग होने के बावजूद दोनों की सत्ता और स्वरूप एक ही माना गया है. इसमें से एक लिंग 'ओंकारेश्वर' यानि (विंध्याचल पर्वत पर) और दूसरा 'ममलेश्वर' या फिर कहें 'अमलेश्वर' (नर्मदा के दूसरे तट पर) स्थित है.
